title: The Bulgarian Alphabet: All 30 Cyrillic Letters
meta_description: All 30 letters of the Bulgarian Cyrillic alphabet with English sounds, the six letters that trick English speakers, and real signs to practise on.
summary: Thirty letters, and most English speakers can read Bulgarian street signs after an afternoon. A third of the alphabet already looks and sounds like English; another third only looks familiar. This guide covers every letter, the six traps, and twelve signs you will actually see.
body:
Thirty letters. Most English speakers can read Bulgarian street signs after an afternoon with this page — because a third of the alphabet already looks and sounds like English, and another third only *looks* familiar.

Bulgaria has a reasonable claim to having invented Cyrillic: it was developed in the First Bulgarian Empire in the 9th century by students of Saints Cyril and Methodius, and spread from there across the Slavic world. It is still marked every 24 May, which is a public holiday.

## The six letters that trip everyone up

Read this bit twice. These look like Latin letters you already know. They are not, and getting them wrong is the difference between reading a sign and guessing at it.

- **В в** is **V**, not B. *Вход* = "vhod" = entrance.
- **Н н** is **N**, not H. *Не* = "ne" = no.
- **Р р** is a rolled **R**, not P. *Ресторант* = "restorant".
- **С с** is **S**, not C. *Сметка* = "smetka" = the bill.
- **У у** is **OO**, not Y. *Улица* = "ulitsa" = street.
- **Х х** is a throaty **H**, not X. *Хляб* = "hlyab" = bread.

And one with no English equivalent at all: **Ъ** is a vowel, a short "uh" like the u in "curt". It is never silent and never a hard sign, whatever you may know about Russian. You meet it immediately — **България** is "Bul-*ga*-ria".

## All 30 letters

| Letter | Name | Sounds like | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| А а | a | a in "father" | Аптека — pharmacy |
| Б б | bŭ | b in "book" | Банка — bank |
| В в | vŭ | **v in "van" — not b** | Вход — entrance |
| Г г | gŭ | g in "go" | Град — town |
| Д д | dŭ | d in "dog" | Дом — home |
| Е е | e | e in "bed" | Евро — euro |
| Ж ж | zhŭ | s in "measure" | Живот — life |
| З з | zŭ | z in "zoo" | Здраве — health |
| И и | i | ee in "see" | Имот — property |
| Й й | i kratko | y in "boy" | Май — May |
| К к | kŭ | k in "kite" | Къща — house |
| Л л | lŭ | l in "lamp" | Лекар — doctor |
| М м | mŭ | m in "map" | Море — sea |
| Н н | nŭ | **n in "no" — not h** | Нотариус — notary |
| О о | o | o in "hot" | Община — municipality |
| П п | pŭ | p in "pen" | Покрив — roof |
| Р р | rŭ | **rolled r — not p** | Ремонт — renovation |
| С с | sŭ | **s in "sun" — not c** | Село — village |
| Т т | tŭ | t in "top" | Ток — electricity |
| У у | u | **oo in "moon" — not y** | Улица — street |
| Ф ф | fŭ | f in "fish" | Фирма — company |
| Х х | hŭ | **ch in "loch" — not x** | Хляб — bread |
| Ц ц | tsŭ | ts in "cats" | Цена — price |
| Ч ч | chŭ | ch in "church" | Чай — tea |
| Ш ш | shŭ | sh in "shop" | Шофьор — driver |
| Щ щ | shtŭ | "sht" run together | Щастие — happiness |
| Ъ ъ | er golyam | **u in "hurt" — a vowel** | Ъгъл — corner |
| Ь ь | er malak | softens the letter before it | Шофьор — driver |
| Ю ю | yu | yu in "yule" | Юли — July |
| Я я | ya | ya in "yard" | Ябълка — apple |

Bulgarian is close to phonetic: letters almost always sound the way they look, so once you know the table you can pronounce words you have never seen.

## Twelve signs you will actually see

Cover the English and sound each one out.

| Sign | Sounds like | Means |
|---|---|---|
| ВХОД | vhod | Entrance |
| ИЗХОД | izhod | Exit |
| ОТВОРЕНО | otvoreno | Open |
| ЗАТВОРЕНО | zatvoreno | Closed |
| АПТЕКА | apteka | Pharmacy |
| БАНКА | banka | Bank |
| ПОЩА | poshta | Post office |
| БОЛНИЦА | bolnitsa | Hospital |
| ТОАЛЕТНА | toaletna | Toilet |
| СПИРКА | spirka | Bus stop |
| ЦЕНТЪР | tsentar | Town centre |
| ХЛЯБ | hlyab | Bread |

## Hear them spoken

Reading is half of it. The [language section](/language) plays every letter, word and phrase aloud in a Bulgarian voice, and [practice](/practice) turns it into a game so it actually sticks.

When you are ready for whole sentences, [Bulgarian phrases for buying a house](/guides/bulgarian-phrases-for-buying-a-house) covers the ones that get you through a first week, plus the questions worth asking at a viewing.

title: Cost of Living in Bulgaria: Real Euro Figures
meta_description: What it actually costs to live in Bulgaria in euro — rent, utilities, food and a realistic monthly budget for Sofia, the coast and village life.
summary: Bulgaria is still among the cheapest countries in the EU, but the gap has narrowed and cheap covers everything from a village at €700 a month to central Sofia at €2,400. Real euro figures for rent and bills, what locals earn, and what is not as cheap as you expect.
body:
Bulgaria is still one of the cheapest countries in the EU to live in — but the gap has narrowed, and "cheap" covers everything from €700 a month in a village to €2,400 in central Sofia.

Since 1 January 2026 everything is priced in euro, at a fixed 1.95583 leva. That makes comparison with home much easier than it used to be.

## A single person, per month

All-in: rent, bills, food, transport and a normal social life. These are Sofia figures — most of the country runs cheaper.

| Level | Per month | What it buys |
|---|---|---|
| Careful | €1,200 – €1,500 | Essentials, flat outside the centre, cooking at home |
| Comfortable | €1,500 – €2,000 | Central one-bed, eating out regularly, private healthcare |
| Generous | €2,000 – €2,400 | Larger flat, a car, travel, no real thinking about money |

Outside Sofia, knock 25–40% off. In an inland village, a couple who own their home outright can live on considerably less than the careful column.

## Rent and bills

| | Sofia centre | Outside centre |
|---|---|---|
| One-bedroom flat | €600 – €750 | €450 – €550 |
| Two-bedroom flat | €800 – €1,100 | €550 – €750 |
| Utilities (85m² flat) | €120 – €150 average, €150 – €200 December to February | |

Rents did not jump at the euro changeover — Bulgarian leases were commonly written in euro long before January 2026, so the switch changed the label rather than the number. Retail and hospitality prices are a different story; plenty crept up during the transition, which is the usual pattern.

## What locals earn, and why it matters

| Figure | Per month |
|---|---|
| Minimum wage (from January 2026) | €620 |
| **Median gross salary** | **~€945** |
| Average gross salary | ~€1,475 |
| Average net salary | ~€1,145 |

That gap between the median and the average is the most useful number here. Most "average salary in Bulgaria" articles quote the average, which describes a Sofia software developer rather than the person serving you coffee in Plovdiv. **Judge local prices against the median.**

The practical upshot: a couple on two modest UK state pensions are, in Bulgarian terms, comfortably above local median household income. That buys a lot of quality of life — and it is also why you should expect foreigner pricing on building work and second-hand cars unless you have a local with you.

Income tax is a flat 10%, among the lowest in the EU. Where you are tax resident and how your pension is treated is a more complicated question than that headline rate suggests — see [tax and finance](/tax-finance).

## What is genuinely cheap

- **Property.** The headline attraction, and still true.
- **Eating and drinking out.** A proper restaurant meal for two with wine is a fraction of UK prices.
- **Fresh produce in season.** Markets are excellent and cheap.
- **Public transport.** City transit and intercity buses cost very little.
- **Trades and services.** Labour is cheap by Western European standards.

## What is not as cheap as you expect

- **Winter heating.** Bulgarian winters are properly cold and older village houses are frequently uninsulated. Heating a draughty stone house can cost more than a modern Irish semi.
- **Cars and fuel.** Fuel is broadly at EU levels and used cars are not the bargain people expect.
- **Imported and branded goods.** Electronics, familiar British brands and specialist food cost the same or more than at home.
- **Serious healthcare.** Routine care is inexpensive, but most foreign residents pay for private cover. See [healthcare](/healthcare).
- **Renovation.** The cheap house is cheap for a reason.

### The renovation trap

The most common expensive mistake is buying a €20,000 village house and discovering it needs €50,000 of work to be habitable through a Bulgarian winter. Budget for a survey *before* you buy, and get quotes from more than one builder. [Renovation](/renovation) goes through what old properties actually need.

## Where you live changes everything

| Area | Relative cost | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Central Sofia | Most expensive | Best hospitals, airport, English widely spoken |
| Plovdiv, Varna, Burgas | Mid | Good amenities at noticeably lower cost |
| Black Sea coast | Mid, seasonal | Lively in summer, partly shut in winter |
| Mountain towns | Low | Beautiful, cold, further from a major hospital |
| Inland villages | Cheapest | Little English, ageing population, a car is essential |

Compare specific areas in [places](/places), and see [costs](/costs) for a breakdown you can adjust to your own situation.

*Figures are indicative, not quotes. They were drawn from published cost-of-living data in September 2026 and will drift. Verify locally before committing to anything.*

For what daily life is actually like beyond the numbers, read [living in Bulgaria](/guides/living-in-bulgaria).

title: Living in Bulgaria: The Honest Version
meta_description: What living in Bulgaria is actually like — the climate, the bureaucracy, the language and the isolation, as well as the mountains and the cost.
summary: Most articles about living in Bulgaria are written by estate agents or by people three weeks into the honeymoon. This is the version that covers the winters, the paperwork and the rural isolation as well as the cheap wine, plus who tends to settle happily and who does not.
body:
Most articles about this are written either by estate agents or by people three weeks into the honeymoon. This is the version that covers the bureaucracy, the winters and the isolation as well as the mountains.

## The short version

**What people love**

- **Cost.** Your money goes dramatically further, especially if you have sold property at UK or Irish prices.
- **Space.** Land and house sizes that would be unaffordable at home.
- **Food.** Markets, seasonal produce and a genuine food culture.
- **Landscape.** Mountains, forest, the Black Sea, very little of it overdeveloped.
- **Pace.** Slower, less pressured, more time outdoors.
- **EU and Schengen.** Full membership since January 2025 — no border checks travelling home.

**What grinds**

- **Bureaucracy.** Slow, paper-based, frequently requiring you to appear in person with documents you did not know existed.
- **Language.** Outside cities and tourist areas, English is genuinely rare.
- **Winters.** Properly cold, and rural houses are often uninsulated.
- **Rural isolation.** Village populations are ageing and shrinking. Some are very quiet indeed.
- **Healthcare access.** Fine in cities, a long drive from a serious hospital in the mountains.
- **Getting things done.** Tradespeople, deliveries and officials run on a different timescale.

## The climate is not the Mediterranean

This catches people out more than anything else. Bulgaria has a continental climate: hot dry summers and cold winters with real snow, particularly inland and in the mountains. The Black Sea coast is milder but has its own problem — resort towns that are lively in August and substantially shut from October to May.

If you are viewing in June, make yourself imagine the same village in February with the shop shut and the road unploughed. Plenty of people buy a summer idyll and discover they have bought a winter one too.

## Bureaucracy is the real adjustment

Not corruption particularly — just process. Things that are a two-minute online form at home are, here, an office visit, a queue, a stamped paper, and often a second office visit because the first office needed something the second one issues.

Two things make it survivable: a good local lawyer or fixer, and patience. Both are worth paying for. Doing residency paperwork, utility transfers and property registration yourself, in Bulgarian, from a standing start is a way to lose months.

## Language decides how well this goes

You can get by in Sofia, Plovdiv, Varna and the resorts without Bulgarian. You cannot really get by in a village — not because people are unfriendly, the opposite generally, but because the person who can fix your roof, the woman at the council desk and your nearest neighbour simply do not speak English.

The people who settle happily are almost always the ones who made a real attempt at the language. You do not need fluency. Reading [the alphabet](/guides/bulgarian-alphabet) and holding [a hundred words](/guides/bulgarian-phrases-for-buying-a-house) changes how you are treated more than you would expect. The [language section](/language) has it spoken aloud, and [practice](/practice) makes it stick.

### The head-shake

Bulgarians traditionally shake their head for **yes** and nod for **no**. People who deal with foreigners often switch to the Western version, so you can never be certain which you are getting. When something matters, ask for the word rather than reading the gesture.

## Healthcare: fine until it is not

Routine care is inexpensive and generally competent, and pharmacies are excellent — Bulgarian pharmacists handle a lot of what would be a GP appointment at home. Most foreign residents take private cover anyway, because it is cheap by Western European standards and removes both the queues and the language barrier.

The thing to plan around is distance. A picturesque mountain village is a long ambulance ride from a hospital equipped for a cardiac event or a stroke. If you are retiring, weigh that against the view honestly — it is the factor people most often wish they had taken more seriously. See [healthcare](/healthcare).

## Community, and being the foreigner

There are established British and Irish communities, mostly near the coast and in particular inland areas. They are a genuine soft landing and also a trap: it is entirely possible to live here for a decade inside an English-speaking bubble, never learn the language, and never quite belong anywhere.

Expect foreigner pricing on building work, second-hand cars and anything negotiated. It is not personal and not universal, but going in with a local who can ask the price before you speak will save you real money. [Avoid scams](/avoid-scams) covers the sharper end of this.

## Who tends to settle, and who does not

| Tends to work | Tends not to |
|---|---|
| Visited in winter before buying | Bought after one summer viewing trip |
| Learned some Bulgarian | Assumed English would be enough |
| Budgeted for renovation properly | Budget was the purchase price |
| Within reach of a decent hospital | Chose the view over the drive time |
| Kept a way back | Sold everything and burned the boats |

## Next

Work out whether the rules even allow what you are planning with [can I move?](/can-i-move), then compare areas in [places](/places) and read [moving to Bulgaria from the UK](/guides/moving-to-bulgaria-from-uk) for the passport and residency detail.

*General impression and orientation, not advice about your situation. Residency, tax and healthcare entitlement depend on your nationality and circumstances. Correct as of September 2026.*
